idiom_name: qualified access modifiers (private[C], protected[C], private[this]) with an enclosing object or package as the grant scope
implementation_notes: Scala puts the restricted grant in the modifier itself: private confines a member to the directly enclosing template and its companion, and a private modifier can be qualified with an identifier C denoting an enclosing class or package, after which the member is accessible only from code inside that class or package - the specification calls this qualified private - with private[this] as the object-private form (Scala 2.13 specification, classes and objects). The idiomatic realization is to place the implementation inside the scope that may see it and qualify the members with that scope, so the nesting is the attorney and every other reference is a compile error. A hand-built forwarding type is still justified when the grant must go to exactly one collaborator rather than to a whole enclosing scope, or when the granted surface must be narrower than the members themselves.
pitfalls: private[C] names a scope, not a type: every definition inside C - including ones added later - receives the grant, so the boundary is an enclosing package or object cluster rather than a single collaborator.

Companion objects and classes of the qualifying scope are inside the grant, and a member marked private[this] cannot even be read from another instance of the same class, which surprises readers who expect class-level privacy.
Scala visibility is largely a compiler-level check: nested scopes have no JVM representation, so the emitted bytecode is effectively public and Java code or reflection can reach what scalac hides.
